speaker: Craig Fuller
title: We're In the Midst of Trucking Bloodbath 2.0
question: In contract trucking markets, why do analysts track how often carriers reject tendered loads rather than relying on freight volume alone?
guest: The tender rejection index measures the percent of freight that is rejected, and the reason that's important is it helps us measure the balance of supply and demand. Looking at volume is only one aspect of it; you also have to look at capacity to understand the metrics of the industry. So we look at the tender rejection index because it tells us how many loads are getting rejected. Think about an airline: you have an airplane with a finite number of seats, and everybody knows that airlines want to overbook that aircraft. That's the goal. Anybody that runs a hotel wants to overbook the rooms, and they're going to intentionally bump some players in that market. The same thing happens in trucking: trucking companies will overcommit to capacity versus what they can actually handle, knowing that at times they're going to have to reject some freight. Back in the peak cycle a year ago, we saw rejection rates as high as 30%.

points.core: Freight volume alone misses changes in available trucking capacity.
points.note: Accept: volume only measures demand, so it cannot reveal market tightness without accounting for supply or truck capacity. Do not credit: generic claims that volume data is noisy or inaccurate.

points.core: Carriers intentionally overcommit contract capacity just like overbooked airlines.
points.note: Accept: fleets overbook contract loads relative to actual truck capacity, similar to airlines or hotels overbooking seats or rooms. Do not credit: claiming carriers only reject loads due to emergencies or bad weather.

points.core: Contract rejection rates directly measure real-time supply versus demand balance.
points.note: Accept: the share of contracted loads turned down shows whether capacity is tight (high rejections) or flooded (near-zero rejections). Do not credit: confusing carrier rejections with shipper cancellations or consumer returns.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Analysts track tender rejections because volume only shows demand, while rejection rates reveal the balance between demand and available truck capacity, which is what actually drives pricing.

Contract freight moves under pre-negotiated rates, but those contracts are generally non-binding: a carrier can decline any load a shipper tenders. Carriers reject loads mainly when they have better options, typically higher-paying spot freight, or when their trucks are simply not available in that lane. So a rising rejection rate signals that capacity is tightening and that contract rates have fallen behind the market; a low rate signals loose capacity and carriers happily accepting whatever contract freight they are offered.

Volume alone can't tell you this. Freight volumes can rise without stressing the market if capacity is plentiful, and a market can tighten on flat volume if carriers exit or drivers become scarce.

Rejections also work as a leading indicator. Rejected loads spill into the spot market, pushing spot rates up, and sustained high rejections eventually force contract rates higher in the next bid cycle. Rejection rates of roughly 5 to 7 percent are often read as the threshold where pricing power shifts from shippers to carriers.

points.why: The response cites better-paying freight and truck unavailability but never says carriers deliberately commit to more freight than they can haul.
The response directly links the rate at which carriers decline tenders to how tight or loose capacity is relative to demand.

Freight volume alone only measures shipping demand, revealing nothing about how much trucking capacity is available to haul it. High volume can move smoothly when trucks are plentiful, while modest volume can still strain a market after carriers exit. Tender rejection rates capture that supply-demand balance in real time.

Because contract trucking agreements fix pricing for months at a time without strictly binding commitments, contract rates adjust slowly to market shifts. Carriers respond first through load acceptance: when capacity tightens or spot market rates climb above contracted prices, they turn down tendered contract loads either because their fleets are already full or to pursue higher-paying spot freight. Rising rejections expose routing-guide breakdowns that force shippers down to pricier backup carriers and into the spot market, making rejection rates an early leading indicator of spot rate spikes and eventual contract rate resets. Conversely, low rejection rates show carriers accepting nearly every load to keep trucks moving, revealing excess capacity and weak carrier pricing power even when overall freight volumes appear healthy.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Analysts watch tender rejections because volume only tells you about demand. What sets rates is how tight capacity is compared with that demand, and rejection rates show this directly. Under a contract, a carrier has agreed to haul a shipper's loads at a fixed rate, but it can still turn down individual tenders. It usually does so when the spot market pays more or when it has no trucks to spare. A rising rejection rate therefore means contract prices have fallen below what the market will pay, and carriers are moving their trucks to more profitable spot freight. Volume can't show this, because the same number of loads can be easy or hard to cover depending on how many trucks and drivers are available.

Rejections also act as a leading indicator. When they rise, shippers fall back to backup carriers and the spot market, which pushes spot rates up and eventually forces contract rates to be renegotiated. Measures like FreightWaves' Outbound Tender Reject Index are updated daily and cover a large share of contracted freight. That makes them a timely, high-frequency read on the balance of market power between shippers and carriers.

models.answer: Freight volume alone measures demand—how much freight shippers want to move—without revealing how much truck capacity is available to haul it. A market with high freight volume can remain loose and inexpensive if carriers have plenty of idle trucks, while a market with flat or declining volume can tighten sharply if enough carriers exit or reposition equipment. Tracking tender rejection rates captures that supply-and-demand balance directly. Because most trucking contracts allow carriers to decline tendered loads without strict penalties, carriers reject freight when their networks are full or when spot-market rates rise enough to make uncontracted loads more lucrative. When rejections climb, declined loads cascade down shippers' routing guides to more expensive backup carriers or spill into the spot market, pushing up rates and signaling that carriers hold pricing power. Conversely, low rejection rates show that carriers are eager to accept contracted freight, indicating excess capacity and downward pressure on rates regardless of raw volume.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Freight volume shows how much freight shippers need to move. The tender rejection rate shows how often carriers turn down loads offered under existing contracts, giving analysts a read on how tight truck capacity is at contracted rates.

The same freight volume can produce very different rejection rates. If trucks are scarce or carriers can earn more on the spot market, more tenders get rejected even when volume is flat. If trucks are plentiful, carriers can accept more loads even as volume rises. Rising rejections can therefore warn that shippers will have to rely more on the spot market, putting upward pressure on rates.

Freight volume shows how much freight shippers want to move. The tender rejection rate shows how often carriers decline loads offered at contract rates. The same volume can be easy to cover when trucks are plentiful and hard to cover when capacity is tight or carriers can earn more in the spot market.

Rejections also help analysts interpret the volume figures themselves. If a carrier declines a load and the shipper offers it to another carrier, that shipment can generate multiple tenders, making tender volume rise even when there’s no additional freight. Tracking both measures helps analysts distinguish demand growth from repeated attempts to cover the same loads and spot emerging pressure on rates.
